["The hon. gentleman who has just

spoken (Mr. Foster) at the conclusion of his speech-which I must characterize as a comparatively moderate speech for him- paid certain compliments to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). Let me at the outset suggest to my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) and the House, that, in my judgment, it has fallen to the lot of few men, in this or any other country, to have occupied the position of Finance Minister for thirteen years with such credit to himself and his country as the present Minister of Finance has done. And let me further say that I doubt if in any country any Minister of Finance ever had the pleasure of presenting to his people so many splendid financial annual statements as my hon. friend has had the satisfaction of doing during his thirteen year's term of office. And I submit that no one who has heard those financial statements from year to year, as I have done, couched in the clear, cheery and eloquent language and reasoning of which my hon. friend is a past master, could fail to see in them the best possible evidence of the progress and prosperity of this country during the term in which this government has held the reins of power, and at the same time the best possible proof of the sound fiscal policy of the present government. I can quite well understand how my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Foster) finds himself considerably handicapped in his attempt to criticise our present Minister of Finance. There is scarcely a fiscal irregularity of which my hon. friend has not been guilty, there is scarcely a fiscal difficulty which he has not gone through, and all I can say is that during his term of office, that term was marked by so many deficits, that he should be the last man to cavil at the fiscal administration of the present government. He remarked that he missed somewhat the tone of hilarity in the present budget speech which the Minister of Finance displayed on former similar occasions. Surely, while others might make a comment of that kind, it comes with ill-grace from the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Foster) who, during the last years of his term, became quite an adept in producing deficits from year to year. He said that this paltry surplus of $1,500,000 in our financial statement for the closing year evoked a cheer from the government benches. Well, during the last three years during which my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) held office as Finance Minister of the late government, what was the condition of affairs which he presented to the country? In 1893-4 we had a deficit of $1,200,000; in 1894-5 our deficit was $4,100,000; and in 1895-6, the deficit was $350,000. So that during the last three years of his admirable management of the financial affairs of this country, the situation was such that we had deficits 146	I i ! 1	'
aggregating $5,700,000. Surely, under these circumstances much of the criticisms to which we have listened from the hon. gentleman to-night, while they might come with some grace from some others, come with rather bad grace from him.
My hon. friend spoke of the Quebec bridge. Can he have forgotten altogether the Curran bridge? And when he spoke of the Newmarket canal, to which he so characteristically referred as the Ayles-worth canal, had we not good reasons to recollect another canal which, if I were disposed to follow the example set by the hon. gentleman, I would call the Haggart ditch.
He talked about our increasing public debt, but he failed to recollect that in the eighteen years of Conservative rule, our debt was increased $118,000,000. My hon. friend talked about this country as a poor country and deplored our piling up the public debt. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not accept that view of this country. While I am one of those who believe that the government should do as they are doing, while I believe that they should curtail our expenditures, so as to suit the existing circumstances and conditions, now happily passing, at the same time I look forward to the future in the most optimistic spirit. I look to a great improvement in our condition. With our magnificent heritage, our splendid resources and rapidly increasing population, I believe that the present financial difficulties will very soon be a thing of the past, and Canada will be again in as good a position financially as that which she occupied a year or two ago. But if we are spending money too rapidly, what are we to think of my hon. friend who made in Prince Edward Island this statement, which I find published in the ' Examiner,' a Conservative paper of that province:
For myself, I stand ready to implement our bargain with Prince Edward Island by the construction of a tunnel.
Why, Mr. Speaker, that would mean an expenditure of two or three million dollars a year, during some years. And what would our expenditure amount to if we began to give to Britain one or two Dreadnoughts, as my hon. friend, in his eloquent speech in this House a few days ago, suggested we should do?
He instituted a comparison between the request of the people for a local work such as the Newmarket canal and the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific. We all know that these local works are started by the petition of a few people in the locality; and in this particular connection, while he seemed to pay special attention to the people of the maritime provinces, he failed entirely to recollect that while in the one", "

case the matter was a purely local one, so far as the eastern section of the Grand Trunk Pacific is concerned, that is a work deliberately entered on by this government, which in 1904 obtained the ratification of the entire people, and was re-endorsed by the election returns in October, 1908. Then my hon. friend-and in this I think he was particularly unfortunate-spoke of ' the land for the settler,' and referred in the most sarcastic way to ' the land for the settler ' under this government. My hon. friend was very rash in many of his statements and suggestions, but in none more than in this. Let us look at the situation, let us make a comparison of the government of which he was a member and the present government on this point. I find, from a return brought down by the Minister of the Interior a few days ago, that under Conservative rule, the railway grants of land amounted to 31,000,000 acres; the total alienations of land other than to settlers, 46,000,000; and the lands for the settler to 7,900,000 acres. On the other hand, under Liberal rule, the railway grants were not thirty-one millions of acres- they were not one acre, and the alienations of lands to other than settlers amount to 7,921,000 acres. But let us come to the settler-and it was as to this that my hon. friend was particularly sarcastic in his reference to this government. We find that, while in the eighteen years of Conservative rule, only 7,900,000 acres of land went to the settler, the Liberal government has in twelve years handed over 23,590,000 acres to the settler. Could anything show more clearly the difference of policy between one government and the other in reference to this very matter which has been so important in the development of the west and of the country at large?
My hon. friend also stated that the credit of Canada was strained. In my judgment, nothing could have been better for the credit of Canada than the annual statements which have been put forward by this government. Year after year it was known and advertised to all the world that Canada was going ahead financially in an utterly unprecedented way. Year after year it was proclaimed abroad that there was a large surplus of ordinary receipts over the ordinary expenditure of the country. Nothing could more authoritatively stamp with approval the credit of the country. Another fact made known to the world was that, through the enlightened immigration policy of this government, millions of people were entering Canada, and particularly the Northwest. Another thing to establish the credit of the country was the fact that, year after year, until last year, the trade of Canada was expanding more rapidly than that of any other country in the world, or at least as rapidly as any. A great deal has been said to-night about the Grand Trunk Pacific. I sometimes feel that we do not realize, that we do not impress upon our own minds with sufficient seriousness, the remarkable work that this government has been doing in connection with transportation during the last 12 or 13 years. We all know that for 30 or 40 years, the project of a 14-foot canal from Lake Superior to tide water has been discussed. I know that as far back as 1865, when a great trade convention was held in Detroit, to which representatives came from all parts of Canada and the United States, the project of a 14-foot waterway from the upper lakes to the St. Lawrence was discussed. Was that ever accomplished? Never until this government came into power. They at once commenced to expend large sums of money for the purpose of making an accomplished fact what had been talked of since 1865, and in 1900", "we had completed a 14-foot waterway from Lake Superior to tide water. Then the government abolished the canal tolls. They dredged rivers and harbours and built wharfs. Then they entered upon the great project of the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway. One would sometimes fancy, particularly when listening to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that is not a road in which the people of this country are interested. Twice we have had the ratification and endorsation of the people of this country of that great project. That road was conceived, as we know, for several nur-poses, first as a continental and imperial transportation road, second as a colonization and developement road for that new Northland, and third for the reduction and regulation of freight rates, and we have been learning on the most expert engineering testimony that what was predicted as one of its greatest features, the four-tenths per cent grade from the foot of the Yellowhead Pass to the sea-board, that is from a point beyond the wheat fields to tide water, will undoubtedly be secured when the road is completed and that we will have a road unequalled in any other country in the world. We have spent, as the Minister of Finance has intimated, a large sum in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have spent $20,000,000 on canals, $30,000,000 on the Intercolonial Railway, $7,000,000 on the Montreal Harbour and River St. Lawrence Ship Channel, we have spent $2,000,000 on the harbours of Fort William and Port Arthur and Port Colborne, and large amounts on many other important works. These large expenditures are necessary in a young and growing country for the purpose of developing the transportation facilities without which it is useless for us to tempt people to come to Canada, because unless we provide the facilities for them to enter the country and to transport their products to market, the great influx of immigrants will quickly cease and this country will not progress as we hope to see it. Then, we are looking to the building of the Hudson Bay Railway, and the new Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) has also taught us to look to the possibility of the deepening of our canals from 14 feet to 18 feet. And, who is there who looks to what we are doing in transportation, and who looks also at the desperate efforts the Americans are making in various directions to compete with us, but must come to the absolute and irresistible conclusion that if we construct an 18 foot waterway canal, for all time to come we will have the people of the United States handicapped in the transportation of grain from the west to the sea-board.

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to what seems to be a more important fact which has developed in connection with this matter in the legislation which is now being considered in the United States and to which he did not advert in his address this afternoon. As my hon. friend knows, the tariff of the United States is being revised. The Payne Bill, in a slightly amended form, has already passed the House of Representatives and is now being debated in the Senate. One very important clause in that Bill which, if it becomes law, and general opinion seems to take it for granted that it will become a part of the tariff, imposes a maximum or increased range of duties against countries which do not give to the products of the United States the most favoured entrance into their markets. Just how the Bill will pass out from the Senate and the House we do not know, but it seems to be taken for granted that that article, in one form or another, will become a part of the tariff. If it does it raises a pretty serious question. Our trade with the United States is a very large trade. In the French treaty there was given a list of 97 articles in reference to all of which the French got the advantage of reduced duties over our general tariff in the Canadian market. When we were discussing that treaty it was said in the House that although this was a large range of articles a great many of them were items in reference to which we would not look for very much competition from France owing to the nature of the articles and to the manufacturing conditions in France. These 97 articles covered, however, a very wide range, and if the United States is to be allowed into our market on those minimum duties with reference to those articles, a very serious state of things will exist. Diminutions of duty ranging from 7 per cent to 50 per cent of the general rate are made in these articles and some of the articles are even below the preferential rate which is offered to Great Britain, so that on the 97 articles in the one schedule and the 12 in the other and the long list of unenumerated articles on which there is a reduction of 2i per cent, if the United States comes into Canada with their trade they will have the advantage of a lessened duty with reference to that wide and important range of manufactured goods and products. I shall not take up time by reading that list. If I did my hon. friends opposite would see in a moment that many of the articles included in that list are articles in which the United States are very large manufacturers and are very heavy competitors with our own and British producers. Take the manufacture of metals, iron and steel and others; the French goods under those items come in under a lessened duty. Then this United States tariff, as I understand it, comes into force automatically. The rate of duty goes on and after a certain time the increase in duty, which I think runs to about 20 per cent, applies to the products of every country which does not give the most favoured nation treatment to the United States.
That is not the law.
I have said that is not the law. I have said that is the proposition.
There is another proposition that the duties that are mentioned are to be the maximum and that any nation giving favoured nation treatment will have a 20 per cent reduction.
And it means exactly the same thing, for the maximum duty is put on a range that will make no difference whether you take it the one way or the other.
I beg pardon.

It is proposed to have a maximum duty and a minimum duty. The country which does not give most favoured nation treatment does not get the minimum duty but is put upon the maximum list and in arranging their duties they arrange the minimum list so as to give themselves a complete protection and they practically prohibit any large trade in the goods of the country which is put upon the maximum list from entrance into the United States market. That, as I have said, raises a very large question. Owing to the operation of the Japanese treaty the Japanese, by virtue of the most favoured nation clause, get the benefit of the reductions granted under the French treaty without any compensation to this country. If the United States adopt the clause to which I have referred, and press for its acceptance by Canada, the alternative is the payment of the maxi-

mum rate on all Canadian goods entering the United States. And, if we feel that the trade is so large and the advantage to us so great that we could hardly refuse it/ then the United States would claim the whole range of the most favoured nation privileges which are not only given to Japan but to France as well. Then, in two months the process would be completed and after the expiry of that time our trade with the United States would be met by the maximum duties.
Of course nothing has been decided yet, but as I understand it the proposition before the United States Senate is that it shall not go into operation for a year.

However that may be, the gravity of the situation will be easily appreciated. We would have to make up our mind whether we will give to the United States most favoured nation treatment on all these lines for which we get from them no concession, or whether we are to refuse the United States that most favoured nation treatment and in consequence have the $96,921,000 worth of goods which we exported in the last fiscal year, subject to the highest and as I believe a practically prohibitive duty. After the elections had taken place in the United States one would have thought that the Payne Bill would Jiave been a scaling down of the average duties, but I have an analysis made by the clerk of one of the committees and I find to my astonishment that the average under the Payne Bill is higher than it was under the old tariff, and particularly so on agricultural products which to a large extent we export to the United States. We therefore have to consider very carefully whether the theory of most favoured nation treatment is the proper one upon which to base our trade arrangements with other countries. The United States do not hamper themselves with it; they sit down alongside of Japan or of France or of Spain or of any other country and they say: 'Here are our products and there are yours, can we make a trade arrangement between ourselves?' They have only to look to what is beneficial between Spain and the United States; they are not hampered with the knowledge that if they give to one country this or that they would have to give the same to another country, and another country, and another country. They are able to act in the straight business way that a man would bargain with another man, and to make an arrangement between individual countries without considering how it will affect others. I am decidedly of opinion that the old method of most favoured nation treaties is entangling and embarrassing, and that it is constantly leading us into difficulties. Now, let me come to the other loans, what we call the permanent or long loans. I have a table here which will show the comparison between the two governments. We have been led to believe that such has been the policy of the Finance Minister since 1897, that we have been great gainers financially in the money mar-

for renewals and extensions, with i of 1 per cent additional if we thought the Bank of Montreal was not able to put through the whole loan and had to associate other banks with it. But this commission of i of 1 per cent, paid when other banks had to be associated with the Bank of Montreal, has been run up to 1J per cent. I do not know, but it seems to me that these are indications, as I stated this afternoon, of the somewhat strained credit of Canada in the old country to-day. The hon. minister (Mr. Fielding) made no provision when he could have made provision, that is when he had immense surpluses. He allowed everything to go on accumulating, then found himself in the market in 1908 and the late part of 1907 with maturing loans and new loans following one another in such dangerous proximity and in such large amounts that the market did just as any market will do-if you appear there too often it will make you pay for your visits. If my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) had taken the right course, the credit of Canada would have insured the loan, and he would not have needed to pay these immense underwriting charges. Why, in _ one of these loans, he pays the underwriters, then he pays a body of men for arranging the underwriters, then he pays the brokers and bankers for assisting the men who arranged the underwriters -a treble charge and amounting to 1} per cent on the whole transaction. It seems to me that this is a matter worth drawing attention to. It seems to me to show clearly that the Minister of Finance, by lack of foresight and of extravagant and reckless expenditure, has put this country into a position where it must pay altogether unnecessarily high for financial accommodation. And my hon. friend taxes some of us on this side with failure in prophecy- with having said that such and such would be the case only to find that it did not turn out in that way. Not many years ago the Finance Minister said, standing in this House and looking forward to the loans maturing in 1910 and 1913:
We shall save a million dollars in the r&-r.ewal of these loans from 1903 to 1910, and maybe more.
He has not only not saved a million dollars, but he has been out of pocket in renewing these loans and the interest at high rates will run on for the term of the loans.
Now, a word with reference to the matter of management of a country's financial business. _ Somehow or other, we are apt to get it into our heads that different principles and different methods are to be applied to the running of a country's business from those to be applied in running the business of an individual or corporation. I think that is a heresy which has much to answer for. In the first place, it induces action on the part of the government which no business man would for a minute under-Mr. FOSTER.
take, and it lays the foundation for laxity of management of government funds and an extravagant scale of government expenditures, which, if the truth were kept close home both by the government and their followers, that the same principle ought to apply in the management of a government's as in the management of a man's or a corporation's business, we should be less liable to the multifold temptations into which we fall, and the multiplied expenses which these temptations cause us.
Now in the case of an individual, or a corporation, or a government, it is true that in each case the individual, the corporation, or the government are the trust-tees of the business that they carry on. The one who has less responsibility and can therefore dare more, is the individual, because, as he says, his money is his own. It is not entirely his own, his wife and family have claims upon it, and he acts and works for them; but he has less responsibility and more freedom. But when you come to a corporation and when you come to a government, it is an absolute trusteeship, and from that idea of trusteeship the corporation is never absent, and the government ought never to be absent. Now a business man, governed by business instincts, on what methods will he carry out his business? Well, he will, in the first place, ponder every outlay before he makes it. The government makes the outlay first and does the pondering afterwards. He will sit down and count the cost, and if he thinks he can afford it, he will undertake it. The government enters into it and counts the cost afterwards.
Take for instance, the Newmarket canal. Will my hon. friend the Minister of Customs say that he, as a member of the government, as a trustee of the people, sat down and counted the cost of that Ayles-worth ditch before he and his government committed themselves to the expenditure? I do not think my hon. friend will say that, I doubt if any single member of the Cabinet can say that honestly. A private gentleman, or a corporation, would have sat down and counted the cost before they entered into the expenditure. They would have asked very naturally the question, [DOT]first, if there was any water there to put into the canal after they built it. They would have asked the very pertinent question, is it necessary at that cost? They would have asked another pertinent question, is it advantageous in proportion to the cost? Did my hon. friend sit down and ask either of these questions? Did any member of the Cabinet? If so, they were lamentably dense a few weeks ago in this House when not a single one of them could tell us what traffic or what trade they ever expected to go over that Newmarket canal after it was built.
Now there is another difference between a

government, the trustees of the people's money, and an individual or a corporation *which is engaged in constructing works for which it has to pay. In times of prosperity when they decide that the work is to be gone on with, they are very careful to get the proper plan worked out, and to have the proper economy exercised, and to have proper supervision, to see that the work is effective. But that is not the way the government does; that is not the way the government did with reference to the Quebec bridge, that is not the way the government did with reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific, even. The Quebec bridge-fancy a business man undertaking the operation which they undertook, and in the way they undertook it! Fancy any corporation doing it unless it were a corporation which felt that it had sufficient influence to put the government behind its back and see it through if it failed, and pay it interest and a dividend for failing! They paid these gentlemen after they failed, paid them their money back, counted by their stock at par, paid them 10 per cent in advance on their stock as a bonus, paid them 5 per cent on their supposed outlay for the stock from the time that they got their stock and saw that they got good round salaries, several of them, during the whole time they were not doing the business, and after having paid them all that, they assumed the debt, took the assets, and the assets are most of them down in the bottom of the river. Now that illustrates the difference between a government, and an individual or a corporation. I need not elaborate the Grand Trunk Pacific, that is a lesson which is alwavs before us, of a government going into a thing without practically a shred of expert knowledge upon which to base their whole scheme, going into it on estimates made by themselves, or by some others for them, which a few years have knocked into small pieces, and the estimates themselves are doubled and in some cases tripled when it comes near to the period of ascertaining the actual cost.
Well, Sir, these are some of the differences between the way this government operates and the way that an individual or a business corporation would operate. The business man has always to consider two things: What is it going to cost me to carry on my business, and can I pay the debt that I owe when that debt matures ? A government seems to be oblivious of the idea of looking much at the probable cost, and as for the day of ultimate payment, it never crosses their mind. Their reply to that is that the country is good for it. I have heard hon. gentlemen opposite say that over and over again. The government -what has it done? And what has my hon. friend the Minister of Finance done? He has taxed to the limit, he has spent to the limit, he has added mortgages additional
and additional to this country, and he has added to the interest burden as well. Taxes-in eleven and three quarter years he has taken $555,000,000 out of this country, $223,000,000 more than the Liberal-Conservatives took out in the last eleven and three quarter years of their regime. Taxes -they were $28,600,000 in 1896, they were $73,300,000 in 1908, an increase of around $45,000,000 in that time.
And to all this we get the flippant answer, 'Oh, the country is good for it.' Now let us analyse that for a moment. What does the Minister of Finance mean when he says the country is good for it, or what does any gentleman mean when he says, 'Never mind the debt, never mind the burden, the country is good for it?' Do the creditors of Canada foreclose on your public buildings, your docks and your wharfs in order to get their interest, or to get their principal paid back to them? Do they foreclose on your forests, on your fisheries, on your mines or on any of the assets of this country? Not at all. When you say the country is good for it, what you mean is that so long as you can tax enough or borrow enough you will get along, and you tax the individual and you borrow, and you lay the burden of the borrowing upon the individual. So when you say the country is good for it, what you really mean is that the individual taxpayer is good for it, and has got to shoulder the whole thing in the long run.
Then, Sir, every individual tax payer in this country has other business to do, other taxes to pay, and other burdens to shoulder. In the first place he has to keep himself and his family, to run his business, to borrow what is necessary for it, to pay interest and pay the principal as well. That is his first burden. Then he has to pay the municipal current taxes. That is his second burden. Then he has to pay the provincial current taxes. That is his third burden. Then he has to pay a tax to every corporation which makes the means of living and the facilities of life better for him, he gets a higher scale of living but he pays for it in one way or another. In addition to that he has to pay the loan burden of municipalities and provincial governments, and to a certain extent, of corporations. Then the Minister of Finance saying Canada is good for it. comes upon the poor tax payer who has all these burdens and loads him up from $5.46 per head to $11 per head in his short regime. Let us get rid of the idea that the country is good for it, an indefinite something which owns nothing, which pays nothing, but let us remember that every bit of this burden falls ultimately upon the individual taxpayer and the individual tax payer in this country to-day is drained and drained heavily, in many cases he is drained to the point of weakness. One

tiling has helped us and saved us to a large extent and will help and save us in the future, the development and product of our arable lands. The Finance Minister spoke this afternoon of 70,000 immigrants from the United States going up into our new lands. These men, with those who come from other countries, are the people who with dollar wheat-to my mind never to return to the old low rate-raising their productive harvest in the great west and putting it into and vivifying every artery of industry and of commerce in this country are its greatest hope-and these men are coming to Canada owing to the policy pursued by the Liberal-Conservative government long before this government came into power, blazing the path, opening the country, and affording means of transportation for our Northwest, that great last west of free or fairly cheap lands, that is the salvation of our country. As I said, the taxation of this country taking it all through, is for a new and a poor country tremendously heavy and this government ought not to press beyond a reasonable point and add to that already heavy burden. We seldom think of the amount of borrowing that is going on in Canada, of the enormous amount of money that is coming into the country. Sometimes we look at that side of the movement only and forget that every dollar that comes into this country, with its yearly accretion, has ultimately to go out of this country. The moment that a million pounds finds its way into Canada and is invested in any way, that moment begins the return stream, of interest first and finally of Principal. I have urged on the Prime Minister such a re-organization of our statistical system as would enable us to obtain from the official publi-tions, statistical information of a practical kind which would be of value to us in our discussions of subjects of this kind, yet to obtain the figures which I am about to give to the House I have had to avail myself of a very excellent little production published by Mr. E. E. Wood of the Dominion Securities Company in Toronto. I find from this that in the years, in Canada, 1904-5-6-7 and 8 the total of bonds issued by governments, municipalities and corporations was as follows:

There were bonds issued for use in Canada. Of these bonds $196,400,000 were issued in 1908. This is a vast sum but it is but a small portion of the money which has been brought into this country. Of Dominion government bonds, provincial government bonds and railway bonds, there Mr. FOSTER.
were running on December 31, 1908, about $802,000,000. All this goes to show the immense amount of money that is coming into this country, and it teaches us as well that beginning immediately and continuing there is to be an immense amount of money that must go out of this country. The issues of Dominion government bonds unfortunately are not for what we might call productive investments. They go to build public buildings, wharfs, Newmarket canals, St. Joseph wharfs, they go to build Quebec bridges which fall down into the water. Some expenditures are not productive but they are of use in the developement of the country. The main point which I wish to drive home is that we must not justify taxation on the ground that the country is good for it, we must remember that it is the country's burden. Our country has within it such resources and such powers that a livelihood for the public who inhabit it is made easy, and poverty cannot be imminent or widespread. But at the same time we must not overburden the individual.
Just one thing in closing-my right hon. friend is proud of his Minister of Finance; he said so in Halifax. He is also proud of his Minister of Public Works; he told us the other night he is now ' PP,' prouder of Pugsley than ever. I suppose that now after my exposition he will be still prouder of his Finance Minister. Far be it .from me to pluck a single feather from the cap of the Minister of Finance, but at the same time there are considerations that we might indulge in in a quiet way in order to prevent the Minister of Finance from becoming too much elated by the pride that his Prime Minister has in his performances. Suppose that good naturedly I should go over a number of these as the ending of my remarks. In the first place the Prime Minister should be proud of the Minister of Finance because in all the history of Canada there has been no Finance Minister who has so completely swallowed all his principles and all his professions, fiscally, financially, and otherwise, as has the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding). Is not that true? The oldest Finance Minister we have Jiving stood true to his fiscal colours. In the dark times when the Liberals held the government of this country from 1873 to 1878, Sir Richard Cartwright stood to his colours; a free trader he was when he went in, a free trader he was when he came out, and if he was not inclined to be so at all times Alexander Mackenzie kept him so. Even staring defeat in the face they would not change their colours; they were consistent. Sir Leonard Tilley and Sir John Macdonald succeeded. They advocated a new policy when they were in opposition; they were told-my right hon. friend told them- it was only a plea for getting in and that they would not put it in force when they

did get in. But they went in and Sir Leonard put his principles of the National Policy into force and the Liberal-Conservative Finance Ministers kept them in force from that day to the day they went out. Then, my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) came in. He was a doughty free trader in the days of opposition; he was a red-hot economist in the days of opposition; he was dead against the National Policy and the principle of protection when he was in opposition; he was death to surpluses; it was Liberal creed and Fielding doctrine in those days that there should be no surplus. But the hon. gentleman came into office and where are his free trade principles now; whither has his rigid economy taken flight; where is his hatred of bounties?-bounties on iron, bounties on steel, duties on coal and the necessaries of life, bounties on twine, bounties on oil, bounties on beet root sugar. He is without doubt the champion swallower of his principles and policy. My right hon. friend has a perfect right to be prouder than ever of his Finance Minister and no doubt, in this case, a fellow feeling makes him wondrous kind. Well, Sir, the Minister of Finance is champion in another respect; he is the champion taxer of Canada. Of all the Finance Ministers that have ever been, no one has gone so deep into the people's pockets, no one has piled up the altars so high with the hard earnings of the people. He found the tax $28,000,000 when he came in; in 1908 he had raised it to $73,000,000. In 11} years he has taken $223,000,000 more than his predecessors in an equal number of years. My right hon. friend must be proud of him in that respect. If I remember well, once on a time in the city of Ottawa in 1893 he held up the flag inviting all and sundry to march up to the citadel and to put out the men who believed in protection, who overtaxed the people and who were extravagant in their methods of government. 'Well, Sir, my friend the Minister of Finance also takes some rank as scalping the thrifty depositors of this country of a part of their interest upon their deposits in order to swell that vaunted suplus of his which he must have. If he cannot get it by changing 16 million dollars from current account to capital account he can take $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 by docking the depositors in the savings banks of one-half of one per cent, and paying them a return upon their money one to one and a half per cent less than he is paying to the foreign money lenders. No Minister of Finance in the history of Canada has ever so fattened and fed the foreign lender and the foreign broker, and no one has ever made it so pleasant for the middleman as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding). I have read the story of the
commissions and the brokerage charges that have been paid in connection with these loans, and no other Finance Minister of Canada has eveT paid as high rates for money in Great Britain as has the present Finance Minister. In that respect also has he a record. He is also-he will not think I am applying it to him in other than the technical sense-he is also the champion spendthrift of Canada. What I mean by that is that he has spent more than any other Canadian Finance Minister. Coming in on the declaration that $38,000,000 was appalling as our annual expenditure, he climbed up last year to an expenditure of $132,000,000, and no other Canadian Finance Minister has ever accomplished such a feat, expenditures commencing with $41,000,000 a year and ending in the year just past with $132,000,000. I am sure my right hon. friend is now proud of the Finance Minister as a spender. And the purposes of this spending-the Quebec bridge, the Newmarket canal, St. Joseph's wharf, not to come nearer home. Go anywhere through this country, and the list is so large, of absolutely useless and wasteful expenditures, gone into without thought-no cost counted until the whole bill was sent in, and then it was paid. And the quality of the expenditures-why, Sir, there is scarcely a thing upon which money can be spent which is not to-day brought within the category _ of Dominion expenditures, and upon which money is not spent. They have gone so far as to advertise for applications for expenditures. My Tight hon. friend remembers the doughty economist in the days of his opposition crusade-Sir Wm. Mulock of the present moment, who was in Ontario his right hand in the matter of strict and rigid economy. My right hon. friend will remember that he made him at one time Minister of Public Works, and he had not warmed the seat of that office temporarily for more than a few hours before he actually issued a circular inviting all members of parliament and unsuccessful candidates to just advise him if there were any expenditures in their constituencies which they would like to have carried out, as he would be glad to know what they weTe.
There is another eminence which the Minister of Finance has. He has promulgated more interesting and misleading fiction as a basis for public expenditures in this country than any Finance Minister I know of. Witness the Grand Trunk Pacific. How certain he was that that would not cost more than $13,000,000 all told to the people of this country. How certain he was that-the outlay would not be more than $51,000,000 as an advance; and to-day his Minister of Railways puts the outlay at $114,000,000 on the eastern division, less terminals, less Quebec bridge, less a lot of other things, and before it is through with $180,000,000 will be nearer the figure. $51,-

000,000 was in the preface of that most interesting piece of fiction that the Finance Minister read to us in 1903, and to which he issued a supplement in 1904. To-day he faces and for the last year he has faced the monsters that he has conjured up- wastefulness, extravagance, maturing debt, fresh debt, and all the horrors of the money market, with temporary loans in almost every bank, with maturing liabilities of millions of pounds cropping up every few months, and with the conditions that surrounded general finance in the year 1908. He faces all these things. Will the monsters destroy him? Has his wand lost its efficacy? Can he send them back to the vast deep from which he summoned them? It remains to be seen. But he is face to face with them to-day. My hon. friend must go into the market right now, in the year 1909, to ask for a loan of $10,000,000 extra for the Grand Trunk Pacific, if the government carries its policy through. He lias got to ask tins year for at least $30,000,000 for the Grand Trunk Pacific and other capital expenditures. That makes $40,000,000 which he has to look for outside in the year 1909. But that does not end it. In 1910, he has $9,000,000 maturing, and he will have to ask another $30,000,000 for the Grand Trunk Pacific and for the Hudson Bay Railway. Why did the Finance Minister omit to speak of the Hudson Bay Railway to-day? The Prime Minister, the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Railways, all are pledged to the building of the Hudson Bay Railway, and the building of it immediately. Why was no mention of that made to-day? I assume that they will implement their promise; I assume that the west will keep them to that promise. They made it in cold blood, when the worst of the financial proposition was before their eyes, and they knew what they were making. The Minister of the Interior will say we are providing for that out of our lands, selling enough at $3 an acre to pay for it. Let me ask the Minister of the Interior: 'You have sold your lands and got some money for them; where is that money to-day?' Spent, every dollar of it; and if you got in the whole of that money, the next year and the year after, every dollary of it would be spent on consolidated fund account; and when you come to build the Hudson Bay Railway for $20,000,000 or $25,000,000, you must get the money by making a loan on the British market. You have started the annuities crusade and you are taking money from the people of this country for that. Where is the money you are taking in? It is a debt of the country. You put it into the consolidated fund, and you spend it on the things I have been speaking about. Where are the savings of the people which have been entrusted to your care-their capital, on which you pay interest? Every dollar of it is spent. It is Mr. FOSTER.
now and always has been a debt of the country. In 1910 there is $9,000,000 of debt maturing and $30,000,000 which will have to be borrowed for the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Hudson Bay Railway, making $39,000,000. In 1911 there is $8,600,000 of maturing debt and $30,000,000 more for the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Hudson Bay Railway, making $38,600,000. In 1912 there is $31,000,000 of maturing debt and $30,000,000 to be borrowed for the Grand Trunk Pacific, making $61,000,000 for that year; and you will go on to 1913, unless you finish the railway and make the borrowings before, and have in that year $3,700,000 of maturing debt and $25,000,000 to be borrowed for the Grand Trunk Pacific. Each year the minister has to go to London for forty millions, thirty-nine millions, thirty-eight millions, sixty millions, and twenty-eight millions or thirty millions, simply for the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Hudson Bay Railway and maturing loans, not taking into account the great expenditures which from year to year press themselves upon the people of this country. By a bit of legislation a day or two ago you pledged yourselves to $2,000,000 which you have to raise in the next ten years for a steamship line between Canada and France. The Minister of Railways has pledged himself to a large sum of money for level crossings. And so each year brings its own new burden. These are the things which will strain .all the revenue you get, and which will use up the surplus, and more to be raised by borrowing.
Then there are your obligations. What do you suppose the Grand Trunk Pacific will cost in the mountain section? How much short of $100,000 a mile will it cost? A great deal has been said to-night about the Grand Trunk Pacific. I sometimes feel that we do not realize, that we do not impress upon our own minds with sufficient seriousness, the remarkable work that this government has been doing in connection with transportation during the last 12 or 13 years. We all know that for 30 or 40 years, the project of a 14-foot canal from Lake Superior to tide water has been discussed. I know that as far back as 1865, when a great trade convention was held in Detroit, to which representatives came from all parts of Canada and the United States, the project of a 14-foot waterway from the upper lakes to the St. Lawrence was discussed. Was that ever accomplished? Never until this government came into power. They at once commenced to expend large sums of money for the purpose of making an accomplished fact what had been talked of since 1865, and in 1900

we had completed a 14-foot waterway from Lake Superior to tide water. Then the government abolished the canal tolls. They dredged rivers and harbours and built wharfs. Then they entered upon the great project of the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway. One would sometimes fancy, particularly when listening to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that is not a road in which the people of this country are interested. Twice we have had the ratification and endorsation of the people of this country of that great project. That road was conceived, as we know, for several nur-poses, first as a continental and imperial transportation road, second as a colonization and developement road for that new Northland, and third for the reduction and regulation of freight rates, and we have been learning on the most expert engineering testimony that what was predicted as one of its greatest features, the four-tenths per cent grade from the foot of the Yellowhead Pass to the sea-board, that is from a point beyond the wheat fields to tide water, will undoubtedly be secured when the road is completed and that we will have a road unequalled in any other country in the world. We have spent, as the Minister of Finance has intimated, a large sum in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have spent $20,000,000 on canals, $30,000,000 on the Intercolonial Railway, $7,000,000 on the Montreal Harbour and River St. Lawrence Ship Channel, we have spent $2,000,000 on the harbours of Fort William and Port Arthur and Port Colborne, and large amounts on many other important works. These large expenditures are necessary in a young and growing country for the purpose of developing the transportation facilities without which it is useless for us to tempt people to come to Canada, because unless we provide the facilities for them to enter the country and to transport their products to market, the great influx of immigrants will quickly cease and this country will not progress as we hope to see it. Then, we are looking to the building of the Hudson Bay Railway, and the new Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) has also taught us to look to the possibility of the deepening of our canals from 14 feet to 18 feet. And, who is there who looks to what we are doing in transportation, and who looks also at the desperate efforts the Americans are making in various directions to compete with us, but must come to the absolute and irresistible conclusion that if we construct an 18 foot waterway canal, for all time to come we will have the people of the United States handicapped in the transportation of grain from the west to the sea-board.

In the second place, the Canadian government entered upon what might be characterized as an international fiscal policy. In connection with the control of power at Niagara Falls, in connection with the Waterways Commission and its work, in connection with tree planting in the west, and in connection with the establishment of several thousand miles of forest reserves on elevated areas, the government are developing a strong policy of conservation of natural resources. These forest reserves are: in Manitoba-in the Riding mountains, the Duck mountains and the Porcupine mountains. In Saskatchewan-in the Beaver hills, the Moose mountains, the Turtle mountains and the Cypress hills; in Alberta-in the Cooking Lake range, Jasper park, Banff park, Kootenay Lake park; and in British Columbia-on the western slope of the Rocky mountains, Yoho park, Glacier park, and a number in the dry area. Again by accepting the invitation of the United States government and sending three very capable representatives of Canada to the Conservation convention at Washington, the government showed its interest in this great question. I understand that the Washington convention recommended that a permanent commission should be appointed for each country, and I hope the government of Canada will at as early a date as possible appoint a good strong commission to deal with that question from a national standpoint.
Before I close I wish to refer to the criticism of the hon. member for North Toronto in regard to the rapid increase of the public debt. It is quite plain that the hon. member practically admits that apart from the requirements of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, the increase of the public debt is very trifling. The hon. gentleman said, according to ' Hansard ' of March 17, 1908, volume 3, page 5181:
In 1887 the public debt was $227,000,090; in 1896 it was $258,000,000; increase in nine vears, $31,000,000.

In 1908 it was $275,000,000 ; increase in twelve years, $17,000,000.
Up to the present time, leaving out 1908, there has been under this government a comparatively small increase of the debt.
So that practically the hon. gentleman's criticism bears upon the large expenditure for the Grand Trunk Pacific. But if he recollects the record of the Conservative government for the years 1884, 1885 and 1886, he will know that that was a period when the Canadian Pacific Kaiiway was under construction, just as the Grand Trunk Pacific is to-day; and during 1884 the public debt was increased $23,695,135; during 1885, $14,245,841, and during 1886, $26,751,414, or a total increase in those three years of $64,000,000. If this enormous increase in the debt of this country in those years, when the Canadian Pacific Bailway was being constructed, was fair and right in the judgment of the hon. member for North Toronto, why is it not equally proper that the debt should be increased now when we are engaged in the construction of another great transcontinental railway?
In my judgment the government has given us a tariff for revenue which is up to date and adequate to our wants; it has adopted a live and progressive transportation policy, an active and satisfactory immigration policy, a policy that attracts capital and impels foreign concerns to come here and build factories, a policy looking to the conservation of our great resources, and a policy that promotes and increases the output of all our great and leading industries. So long as the government continues the advanced and progressive policy which it has given to this country for the past twelve or thirteen years, so long will the right hon. gentleman who leads the government and the members of the cabinet who surround him retain the confidence of the people, and each time they go to the polls they will receive the popular endorsation which was given to them in October, 1908.
